comments.name: Brian Harvey
comments.body:
I agree that it's important to teach people to be ethical, starting early. But in the particular case of school cheating, the entire practice of assigning grades teaches students that what really matters to us is the grade rather than their learning.  This is especially true in the case of "high stakes testing," a strange name for a practice in which the student has no stakes; it's the *teachers* whose pay is determined by the results of those tests.  And sure enough, when high stakes testing is used, the teachers cheat!  If that's how grades affect teachers, why should we expect students to be any different?

Some time ago I observed classes in an elementary school that spent the two weeks before the No Child Left Behind tests prepping students with worksheets copied from the actual test they would soon be taking, with minor changes in numbers (for the math part) or wording (for the reading part).  The students knew that the teachers were cheating.

If we really cared about student learning, we wouldn't give grades, or used standardized tests.  One great result of teaching this way is that when you feel the need to give a *diagnostic* test, because you're not sure how well the students are understanding some topic, they don't cheat, because they're not being graded and they know the point of the test is to help you teach them.

All this is doubly true if you want to teach ethics.  You can't *grade* students on what they say about ethics and expect them to tell you the truth!

I've come to the conclusion that the only way to stop the vast majority of cheating is to block the behavior.  I have switched to in person, pen and paper exams for all of my classes. My hope is that if we can block opportunities to cheat, students will go back to learning.  My experience so far is that I get significantly more students dropping, but the ones who stay are generally grateful and feel the class was of value. 

Now I am focusing on clear and early communication about how evaluations will be done in order to get more to realize early that their only way through my course is effort.  The challenge is that none of my colleagues in my department do what I do or seem bothered by the near 100% cheating in "online evaluations".  Plenty of colleagues in Math and other STEM areas have had the same realization as I and have been doing pencil and paper in person exams as soon as we could go back to in person instruction.  
I don't claim to have all the answers, but going back to basics seems to make it easier for me to sleep at night.
David, California Community College Teacher

comments.name: Donna
comments.body: I have been a fan of Dolly's since age 7 when I saw her perform at the local county fair. She was not famous yet (circa 1967) but she was already shining as the new 'girl singer' for Porter Waggoner's weekly TV show. People from the Appalachian part of Tennessee (I am one) knew she was authentic and many had grown up as poor as Dolly had. We did not think of her as this 'other worldly superstar'. We saw her as one of us who had stayed true to herself, and used her natural intelligence to realise her dreams. We deeply respected her as she gave back generously and often to the people of her home region as well as other humanitarian causes. She came often to her home region, especially when disasters struck and without being asked for help. For those who are not from Appalachia, local music has always been a part of our daily life, and having a writer like Dolly tell our story to the world was really what endeared her to us. I now live in the UK and the only way I can explain how important she was to us is that she was our equivalent to the UK's Queen Elizabeth II (who reigned over 60 years). We had Dolly for a little over 60 years as our voice. We grieve for her and celebrate her as one of us 'who did good'.

comments.name: Judith
comments.body:
The real threat to free speech isn’t speech we dislike. It’s giving the government the power to decide who can speak, who should be censored and removed. In this administration, dissent isn’t allowed.

French is right that defending someone’s right to speak doesn’t require defending the speaker or the idea. But his comparison falls short when private social pressure is placed alongside government power. The two aren’t equivalent.

People can criticize or ignore speech they dislike. Government retaliation is something else entirely. When political power is used to silence dissent, free speech becomes conditional.

When government decides which voices are acceptable, dissent itself becomes the offense.

comments.name: Mary Sweeney
comments.body: It's important to understand that government interference in free speech is in a category by itself. No one in their right mind would argue that everyone everywhere should be able to say whatever they please whenever they please with no consequences whatsoever. For example, if an employee routinely answers the phone at their workplace by saying, "You've reached Widgets, Inc., they cheat on every contract," that person will likely be fired and will have a hard time contesting that firing. Similarly, an economics professor who thinks women can't do math should not have a job teaching students, since that person's own beliefs are very likely to interfere with his ability to do his job. And we all have the right to control what gets said in our own homes and to ask troublesome guests to leave. These examples are different from a publicly elected government official who tries to punish citizens who dare to criticize him. It is virtually impossible to have a modern, democratic nation in which citizens are not allowed to criticize the government.

comments.name: Dan Shiells
comments.body:
The temporal messages of kindness and tolerance espoused by Christ in his Sermon on the Mount, would be denounced today as "woke" by the right. All it ever said was there are people who face institutional bias and suffer as a result and that this bias is baked into the cake of America. Even extending it to promote proactive methods to compensate would fit well with Christ's message of universal brotherhood and compassion. Diversity, equity, and inclusion are all concepts Christ urged his followers to pursue.

Unfortunately, however benign the intent, woke was taken too far, becoming exclusionary and intolerant in its own way. Chants like Defund the Police and Black Lives Matter, while inspired by legitimate concerns of racial inequity, were ultimately as rooted in anger, misunderstanding, and exclusion as the institutional bias they were fighting. It made it easy to condemn in its totality without acknowledging the value in its attempt to improve the human condition -- even to the point of denying critical scientific evidence about climate change. None of this makes it wrong to acknowledge the reality and impact of institutional bias or to seek ways to make amends.

The right grossly thus misrepresented and savagely caricatured woke and that caricature became the straw man used to attack the left, but sadly that caricature also became the definition generally accepted by the left, as AOC's comment have made apparent. Ms. Cottle's explaining to Mr. Bouie why he was misinformed on woke or perhaps even naive was, frankly, repellant but at the same time revealing of this shared distortion and a lack of rigor.  Cancel culture specifically, whether from the left then or the right now has nothing to do with woke. 

Anti-Wokism is just another example of the right distorting reality then getting mad about its distortion and making political hay with it.

comments.name: Blanche White

I think much of what passes for the entertainment industry is bad for anyone including the consumer.

I remember decades ago at the office I worked in, there was a person hired for the front desk. She was only about 22 and very striking in appearance.  Many asked her if she ever had wanted to be an actor or model.

She explained that she did do a bit of local modeling on the side for extra money but she didn't want that kind of lifestyle and she had a boyfriend that she had long set her sights on.

Her dreams came true. Every bit of it.  She called me last year to tell me how they had sold their home in a good market and lived in a camper on a small tract of land with a pond they had while they built a small house on it, doing much of the work themselves because she remembered how I had done the same thing and was inspired to take on that challenge and be debt free.

When I think of ways to live, I always think of that young girl, smart, and not tempted by tinsel who knew what to value.  I count myself honored to be one she remembers after thirty years.  

What I am unable to understand is why something so simple is so hard to understand for the majority of people who keep buying one sales pitch after another that keeps them forever in the ditch. 

In a sane world there would be no influencers.

comments.name: Peter McKenna
comments.body:
Climate has progressed for millennia. During the Last Glacial Maximum ~20,000–22,000 years ago, ice sheets covered much of North America, including the New York area under a thousand feet or more of ice. The subsequent Holocene warming opened vast regions to habitation, agriculture, and complex societies. Calling this shift mere “change” or crisis understates its directional benefit for humanity.
Activists often claim warming intensifies tropical storms. Yet records show no clear long-term rise in overall cyclone frequency, mixed evidence on intensity, and death rates from weather disasters down more than 90% over the past century despite quadrupled population. That decline stems from forecasting, infrastructure, and technology powered largely by fossil fuels—the same energy system blamed for recent warming.
“Climate progress” is a clarifying frame. It acknowledges human contributions to current warming and local costs, but places them inside a longer history where post-glacial opening of the planet and rising adaptive capacity matter as much as projected hazards. Preferring a permanent ice age would have left humanity poorer and more vulnerable.

It hardly needs to be said, but clearly none of these people deserved such a fate.  Who is responsible?  Is it just a matter of chance and being in the wrong place at the wrong time?  Or if climate change is implicated, do we who use fossil fuels ultimately bear some responsibility for such disasters, as well as for the horrible forest fires that have occurred in Europe, Canada, the northern U.S., and other places?  Is it a combination of bad, dumb luck and preventable conditions caused by our actions?

Whatever the explanation, it's clear these people didn't deserve such a monumental disaster, a reminder that this universe can be coldly indifferent to human affairs, and that it is up to us to seek justice and to relieve suffering whenever possible.  Those efforts, rather than to foment hatred and divisiveness, should give meaning to our lives.

I would urge readers to support relief efforts in this uniquely beautiful part of the world, whose culture and values have much to teach us.

The game rule was to ask everyone yes or no questions to guess who you are -- an icebreaker. Hum, how did I happen to get Dolly Parton written on my back? It wasn't that difficult to guess.

Visiting her pumpkin sculpture on the pier at Naoshima was also a delight. 
Thankful for her art and wit.

comments.name: CB
comments.body:
By happy accident, I went to the Love Forever show at MOMA when I was visiting New York in 1998.  I just loved her work from the first time I saw it and kept the program, which I normally never do.  I am looking at it right now.

I am so glad that she took up art again after that because she had a lot more to say.  I got to go recently to the museum in her hometown of Matsumoto and see the pumpkins and infinity rooms and collection of older work.  Everything is just so captivating. She was a visual genius!

comments.name: enrique cortes
comments.body: I visited Yayoi Kumasa´s infinite room at the Guggenheim Bilbao on a very crowded day, and you had to queue to enter. I queued 5 times, it was that amazing!  We´ll miss her incredible creativity.

comments.name: Stephanie
comments.body:
For all the issues about Kusama's racism, people need to keep in mind that she grew  up in Japan in the 1930s and 1940s where she would not have known or even encountered any Black people.

However, she would have been exposed to a lot of racist images of and writings about Black people that were prevalent in Japan in those days.

Unfortunately, the time she spent in New York seems to have solidified those early idea about Black people, probably because those attitudes were still common in the US at that time.

To put it in context, I believe people need to imagine the thinking of someone white who spent their childhood in the Deep South in the 1930s.

comments.name: Plimsoll
comments.body:
I belonged to a book club for 17 years.   I loved it.  I tried hard and I never interrupted anyone.   I made my comments brief, but I felt they were a contribution.   Finally a member of the group sent an email and said about me, age 67:
"I think Plimsoll is autistic.  When I worked with kindergardeners they exhibited some of the same behavior she does". 

OK!  No more book club for me and I hated that woman's presumption:  she was a much newer member than I was.   They did invite me to join the group because I had written a popular book that was a selection of the BOMC.  Although I had a Ph.D., I never spoke "academic" to them.

And I remain devastated because I had thought they were friends.   Mean girls at every age....

comments.name: IC
comments.body: To "Sarah," who thinks children should be "protected" from people with different morals and values: such an approach does a great disservice to the child and, multiplied enough times, society. Children should learn early on that they share a world with people who have different perspectives, values, priorities, etc. They should learn early on that just because someone differs greatly in their opinions doesn't automatically mean they're "bad" or "evil." In fact, it's a good thing to be exposed to other ideas, especially those you disagree with. The alternative (cutting off contact) will ensure the child grows up self-righteous and utterly unable to comprehend others' viewpoints because they've only ever been exposed to strawman versions of them.

comments.name: JoanMarie
comments.body: Yikes! - to the lady complaining about the slow Mahjong player.  I play golf with a group of 40 women once a week in the summer. On any given week, about 35 golfers will participate.  The group ranges in age from mid-50s to early-80s.  Two of the ladies who are 80+ are very slow for two reasons - they take more shots per hole than the average player in our league and they move at a slower pace when getting out of the cart, selecting their club, and walking to their ball.  Is it frustrating sometimes - sure.  Are we going to kick them out of our league - absolutely not.  We all hope that if we are playing golf into our 80s that we are surrounded by understanding friends who will play with us.

comments.name: Danny Swarzman
comments.body: I've directed tournaments of another board game. We always have players at the bottom rung. Players who are matched against them don't have the same challenge. So what? Their sacrifice allows the tournament to go on. It allows for inclusion. To exclude people threatens group cohesion more than putting up with their idiosyncrasies does. The Mahjong group should organize their play so that the slow player doesn't always play with the same opponents. Share the burden. Excluding players will lead to more unhappiness.

comments.name: Richard
comments.body:
It's amazing to me that commenters here so readily offer advice to the sister who cut off contact with her parents.  The truth is, we know very little about the actual family dynamics in this case, nor do we know what actually took place between family members.  This is may even be true for the LW, who will never know the true and full experiences of her sister.

I had difficult parents, one who was mentally ill and the other who was cold, critical, distant, and judgmental.  I never cut off contact with them, and indeed I actually served as the caretaker for one of my parents during the last decade of their life.  

Did I do the right thing?  Who knows?  I honestly don't know if my maintaining contact and enmeshment with their lives was a sign of weakness or compassion...or maybe just following societal conventions.  But I certainly can understand why some people would choose to cut off contact with their parents.

comments.name: Sheldaine
comments.body:
The mah jongg bully doesn't even realize the irony: "We're kind but we have limits." "We've been friends for years but now you're not playing according to non-existing group rules so we don't want you."
Specifically: "How do we gently tell her she is no longer welcome? We’re kind people; no one wants to hurt her...."
She mentions "accommodations" yet no one in the group has made any accommodations to allow this woman to continue to play at, or near, the desired (arbitrary) speed. Sure, it's frustrating, but imagine how it feels for the player in question. 
Talk to the player and ask how her participation can be enhanced. How she plays is quite possibly frustrating for her too. (Mind you, knowing *your* stance on the issue, and knowing you represent the feelings of the group, I might just decide to leave the group.)

comments.name: Beth
comments.body: There is a reason that one of the 10 commandments is honor your father and your mother. And it’s not to scold back talking teenagers either. It’s because throughout history adults have found their older or elderly parents annoying and prefer less contact or -hey better yet - no contact! But I observe with friends who have experienced this how much bewilderment and pain estrangement from their adult children causes. It violates an important social contract. And it really isn’t nice. So maybe don’t be mean and call your mom or dad and chat a bit.

comments.name: Linda
comments.body:
My Mom was involved in a similar situation. She played bridge with 3 other women for many years. My Mom had smoked cigarettes for 41 years but had stopped around 14 years prior. After she stopped smoking she got an irritating and persistent cough. She was not sick, but she would have coughing fits. She went to a doctor and there was nothing he could do.

This apparently bothered one of the other players greatly. She was greatly bothered by my Mom's coughing. Eventually, they kicked my Mom out of the group. My Mom was devastated and angry. Playing bridge was an integral part of her life and got her out of the house and socializing with others.

One of the women disagreed with the decision to exclude my Mom and they remained friends and would have lunch together here and there until my Mom died.

But I want to reiterate: my Mom was devastated. Crushed by how callously she was treated.

I had a similar situation with a group of women I golfed with at a small club. One woman was difficult to play with. Nobody wanted to ride in a cart with her in our Tuesday morning golf league. She would 'shush' you when she was teeing off even if you were whispering at a great distance. She was a slow player. She never said thank you for anything. She was actually rather cruel sometimes. 

But she was a member, so she had the right to play. So we all took turns riding with her. We were there to have fun and sometimes she would just squeeze the fun out of playing.

Grace. Patience. We played on.

comments.name: A Reader
comments.body: Ms. Gottlieb, if you're reading these comments: to what do you primarily attribute your extraordinarily high level of emotional intelligence? Did it develop organically as a result of inherent temperament, or was it mainly a result of the environment and family in which you were raised? Thanks for sharing if you care to.

comments.name: D Mitchell
comments.body: There are some questions that either need a yes or no answer before further discussion. If you can’t say yes or no, maybe whatever you do say is not going to be helpful. I get the sense that this is one of those situations.

comments.name: Grant
comments.body:
It’s unclear whether the daughter actually had an abortion or not. Two years later the mom “realized”, and that’s her basis for knowing (full stop) that “my daughter had an abortion”?

Maybe, maybe not. 

The therapist’s advice is good in acknowledging that the mom doesn’t actually know, but we don’t know either. The mom feels like she has a way of overlooking hard truths. Ok, that’s something to work on. Whether or not this was one of them, we (and she) just don’t know. 

And you’re allowed to not know. I think that knowing is harder than we think.

Honestly, I think we’d all be better off to just acknowledge what we don’t know, rather than congratulating ourselves for what we think we “know” (and how much righter it is than other people who “know” a different conclusion), or beating ourselves up for imagining that we should have known.

Best wishes to the mom and daughter.

comments.name: Jeff in CT
comments.body: Sometimes when a child, even adult child, asks a difficult question the best response is “why do you ask”. It opens the door to a deeper conversation and informs if it’s a hypothetical, a question about them, or perhaps a friend. The therapists response is spot on if the goal is to improve communication going forward.

comments.name: Susan N.
comments.body: There are an awful lot of snarky comments directed at the mom. Her response at the time--about it being *her grandchild* was clearly inappropriate and obtuse. That said, she's trying to repair something that she damaged and she has a right to try to do that. Someone said fewer words are better. I agree. Make an overture. Express a desire to be present for your daughter. Tell her you realize you've made mistakes. The daughter can take it from there.

comments.name: Kathy
comments.body: It is sad to realize that even to this day abortion is surrounded with secrecy and at times shame.  Abortion and the choice to carry a child are hers and hers alone.  It is unfortunate that it is treated as such a taboo subject that as women we pass each other in the night missing opportunities to connect and share our experiences.  There are many of us that carry in the pit of our stomachs the word "abortion".  I have friends that I have known for 20 years and longer and it is never mentioned.  Enough said.

comments.name: Pipa Francis
comments.body: Awesome, insightful and positive thoughts. They gave me pause which, I think, means I have my own, perhaps not wanting to be acknowledged, tendancies that need to be addressed. So, thank you and ..ouch. As a mother of six, I have had many a salutary lesson from my now grown children. We can only do our best on a daily basis, hopefully learn,  rinse and repeat.

comments.name: Humanist

I can see the mom mentioning some wistfulness re the fetus *after* a longer supportive conversation about difficult decisions, but being unintentionally pregnant is scary enough in this era of low- to no-bodily autonomy for girls and women without your adult role model piling on.

comments.name: CM
comments.body:
I tend to be suspicious of artists who find it necessary to write lengthy explanations of what they were trying to do. As Yoda observed, "Try not. Do or do not. There is no try." No explanation of why "complicated" is a plausible translation for the Greek can make it a poetic choice.

Fitzgerald's translation, here as elsewhere, is peerless:

"Sing in me, Muse, and through me, tell the story
of that man, skilled in all ways of contending,
the wanderer, harried for years on end,
after he plundered the stronghold
on the proud heights of Troy"

This is poetic, musical and propulsive. Anyone who hasn't read it should give it a try.

comments.name: Rodrick Wallace
comments.body:
Another consideration: different translations may vibe with different people. Just based on the two examples of the opening line of The Odyssey, I would prefer the Fagles translation over Wilson's. Historic ballads are still being created among the traditional musicians of Crete and keep alive the old ways of memorializing important events such as the rebellion against the military dictatorship of the 1960's-early 1970's. "Tell me about a complicated man" would be foreign to them.

Part of the appeal to me of certain translations is the sense that they have some resemblance to how the original audience experienced the original work. Translating the Aeneid in high school Latin class and the Roman comedies in college underlined for me the importance of trying to understand the culture of origin.

comments.name: Hillside

comments.name: Brad
comments.body:
Don’t read Wilson’s.  Read Daniel Mendelsohn’s. Here’s one example of how his is better:

In the Odyssey Homer often refers to the dawn. In Mendelsohn's it’s beautifully rendered, “then morning-born Dawn touched the sky with her fingertips of rose.” In Emily Wilson’s it loses all beauty and poesy, “Soon Dawn appeared and touched the sky with roses.” Hers is flat.

comments.name: OWL
comments.body: Dolly Parton was NOT an icon, she was a real flesh and blood person, and certainly not a saint. Just by being who she was, becoming who she wanted to be, she said, “Look, folks, it ain’t that hard to do the right thing.” She didn’t and still doesn’t just test the limits of the south; the south and the country is not a monolith, nor is it neatly divided by lines that wall off some places as less than, or into colors on opposite sides of the color wheel. She said things people all over might object to. It will be a shame if we make her into only an icon and saint, something we can pretend we cannot be. She was and remains an artist, a flesh and blood woman whose art was living well and taking others along for that ride.

comments.name: lh
comments.body: You hear "sorry for your loss" often, and yes, it applies when people lose their loved ones. But to me, not particularly a fan of her music or movie roles, liked them but was not smitten with them, I feel like we mourn as a nation the loss of one of our most wonderful role models and emblems of America, both its gritty reality and the beauty and allure of the so-fragile American Dream. She was a star performer, but she was a truly magnificent human being. It feels like a little more goodness has left the world when we need all the goodness we can muster.

comments.body: My aunt lives in FL. She was in car accident two years ago, almost 3 in which she lost the ability to walk. All she owns is a mobile home. It took her almost 2 years to be enrolled in Medicare. Two years to receive some kind of disability payment and more than two to be able to have a home attendant. My cousin became the caretaker and just recently was able to go to work again. Physical therapy has helped her regain some mobility, but it is so limited that she hasnt been able to fully walk. Medicare is horrible here. Now, we see why the process can take so long. Hope we can see justice before Trump decides to give both of them a pardon.

comments.name: Eugene Gorrin
comments.body:
Per the article, James Uthmeier, who was Governor DeSantis’s chief of staff at the time and is now Florida's s AG, was central to the transactions investigated by the grand jury. 
Asked about the report, Uthmeier suggested without evidence that Democrats had been behind the leaked report and called the investigation a “hoax.”

“Nobody did anything wrong here,” he said. “There was not even probable cause to move forward.”

Really?  Nothing wrong?  A hoax?  And he blames the Democrats for leaking the report?  $10 million went from a Medicaid contractor, who overbilled and settled with the DeSantis administration, to the Hope Florida Foundation.  Then the Foundation distributes the $10 million to 2 nonprofit committees (i.e., "dark money groups").  The 2 groups then routed $8.5 million to Keep Florida Clean, a PAC created to oppose legalized marijuana.  Then the PAC sends $10.5 million to the Florida Republican Party and $1.1 million to the Florida Freedom Fund, which is DeSantis' PAC.

What did "Deep Throat" say to Bob Woodward  in the movie "All the President's Men" about the investigation of Watergate:  "Follow the money."  

Well, follow the money.

Governor DeSantis needs to resign as FL Governor.

Uthmeier needs to resign as FL AG.

Ashley Moody, who was then FL's AG and is now FL's junior Senator and running for election in November needs to resign as Senator and end her campaign.

Political corruption can be brought to light by examining money transfers. It's here.

comments.name: Mel Dallas

Young writers are hot because they have creativity, but often the creativity is just wild derivative imagination based on television. Good fiction comes from living experience, not from watching TV or Google searches.

comments.name: DL

comments.name: Paul

comments.name: IL Ath
comments.body: So much frustration in these comments, and for good reason. Ever wonder what would happen if the penalty possibilities were expanded by adding such corporate activity to the criminal code making boards and top management personally culpable?  It seems like there was intent, a key component of criminal prosecution. The counter-argument, of course, is that would stifle innovation and risk-taking, though the real result might just be more measured innovation without causing so much harm, while still allowing these people to fairly make more money than they could ever spend.

comments.name: r
comments.body: Absolutely will not hope.  Free will leads to the choices one makes and how they let themselves be influenced.  Parents need to take a look at themselves.

comments.name: Christian
comments.body: I’ve learned with my 3 and 6 year olds that PARENTING is the only real solution. It’s easy to blame TV, the phone, the iPad, other people’s kids, the junk snacks they hand out at school…but parenting can squash all this.  Don’t let “the village” raise your child!

comments.name: Thomas Kilbourn
comments.body: I do not understand the celebration regarding Meta's settling the court case.  The monetary figure is insignificant for Meta.  What the settlement means is the larger public does not get to learn about the dehumanizing methods Meta (Facebook) has used from the earliest days, even at Harvard.  The settlement protects Meta, not children.  The time limits et al are utterly meaningless.

comments.name: K
comments.body: Its a tiny shuffle in the right direction as the tech industry sprints ahead.  The real issue is that screens in general are too addicting - not just for teens but the large majority of us (quitting the NYT spelling bee was harder for me than giving up nicotine).  Tech has completely infiltrated our lives for the worse. We are all hooked, we are all spending too much time tapping a screen instead of challenging ourselves, connecting, or even just being bored.  Now throw in AI and we are willingly giving up our jobs and ability to think.  I hate to be a cynic but we’re doomed.

comments.name: Oedipa Maas
comments.body: Their entire ecosystem runs on negative emotional states. Fear, anxiety, inadequacy, envy, outage. Those emotional states are the most monetizable and keep you scrolling, engaging and looking for more content. Haugen testified in 2021 the company understood this and confirmed algorithms move people from positive content to negative content because it makes them more money. They know this and decided not to fix it because it costs them engagement. It’s not just kids it’s every brain on their platforms.

comments.name: Xoxarle
comments.body: Meta sacrificed a quarter's profits ($17B) for a return to business as usual. They don't care about the harm done to kids, they never did. They don't now. They are in business to make money, period, and they make money from engagement and data mining for advertising purposes. Their leaders have grown obscenely wealthy from that. They didn't suddenly grow a conscience in the last 24 hours. They don't even have to admit culpability for all the ugly deception they engage in, in secret, when whistleblowers aren't giving evidence or interviews. Lying to Congressional committees. Supressing internal research. Refusing to implement safeguards over the years because of the threat to revenue. Refusing to modify algorthms to make them less toxic. Refusing to adequately moderate content. Refusing to address dangerous lies and misinformation that get an audience of millions or billions.

comments.name: Right of Way
comments.body: What a joke! Users will find endless and abundant workarounds. Who is kidding whom here?

articles.title: Will Meta’s Changes Benefit Young Users’ Mental Health?
articles.byline: Nina Agrawal and Roni Caryn Rabin
articles.summary: Psychologists said the changes were a symbolic victory, but warned their effectiveness might be limited.

comments.name: Simone
comments.body: I was just a kid when the Moonies came into being. After hearing my parents talk about it I always thought a cult to be a very bad, dangerous thing. Like Q-Anon and MAGA. I’ve never been to a Trader Joe’s. Now I’m afraid try.

comments.name: Howard Schneider
comments.body:
When I read (not in this article!) such orotund rhetoric as the "cult of Costco" or the "cult of Pilates, I assume the writers are being hyperbolic in order to playfully remind readers that some very mundane phenomena have achieved grandiloquent places in our culture. We really shouldn't lose our sense of humor about such semantic shenanigans.
     Moreover: I was somewhat unhappy about Ms. Haigney's statement that "Most people recognize that a devotion to ... James Joyce can be more feverish than is natural." I'm bothered by the word "feverish." Yes, a feverish devotion would be unnatural (I guess), but I perceive that the subtext of that remark is that Joyce's admirers misguidedly overrate him. Alas, I'm one of those misguided people who believe that Joyce is a great writer, an astonishing virtuoso of the English language. As his biographer Richard Ellmann wrote over 60 years ago, "We are still learning to be James Joyce's contemporaries, to understand our interpreter." That's still true.

comments.name: Richard
comments.body: Surely even those who misuse words so flagrantly must recognize the origin of the word cult and its proper use in context. Whomever referred to shoppers at Trader Joe's as a cult is stupid beyond the pale.  It is most peculiar that the writer chose to skip over the most prevalent and dangerous cult in the United States today; the Republican cult of MAGA. The cult like vision of MAGA Republicans has practically every  journalist, judge, election volunteer, university professor, living in fear of being sued, harassed, or attacked by masked men, less they praise their fearless leader. If you want to make a point about the depth of contemporary meaning of a word, try not to avoid the blatantly obvious contemporary meaning on the minds of millions of people.

comments.name: Sarah
comments.body:
The internet has led to mass psychosis with cult like thinking. We see this in the tiktok videos that have convinced a large horde of women that the woman currently on trial for killing her children (she admits it) isn’t actually guilty.

I don’t have TikTok or other social media (please don’t pedantically chime in that NYT comment section is social media.), but I’m aware of what’s going on culturally that is caused by apps like TikTok.

And there is definitely a strong element of consumerism combined with these cults. Stanley cups, Labubus, etc. 

The biggest mass psychosis I watched in my own house was my apolitical husband who use to vote for liberals, he’s not convinced that Trump is saving America. Staring at Facebook and YouTube and watching the pablum roll in passively destroyed his critical thinking. I see it in liberals too, but the right is much more hateful. I hate all of it.

comments.name: Strix Nebulosa
comments.body: The revision of the word "cult" parallels a similar effect with the words "iconic" and "polarized."   An icon used to be something symbolic, like the Statue of Liberty or the Warhol image of Marilyn Monroe, or the Eiffel Tower.  Now it means anything or anyone even remotely famous.  Indeed not even fame is necessary; it only needs to be something we've all heard of, like "Gilligan's Island."    "Polarized" used to mean at either of two extremes, as in the North and South Poles.   Now, in politics, it only means strong division and disagreement, as if everybody is either a Trumpite or a Bernie Bro and there's nobody in between.  All the subtleties in word definition are so tiresome; we need to use any word we want to mean anything we want.  It's a free country, isn't it?   Be careful of that inflammable gasoline can...

comments.name: SR
comments.body: What it used to mean was "a religion that hasn't gotten so big that you're not allowed to question its legitimacy."

comments.name: Jeff
comments.body:
I once asked a therapist to explain to me the difference between a religion and a cult. He gave me a useful mnemonic: you can easily leave a religion, but you can't easily leave a cult--not without enormous peer pressure and ostracism, if not physical danger. If you were part of the "cults" of Taylor Swift or Costco and then left and disavowed them, absolutely no one on the "inside" would care one way or the other, much less try to stop you. 

So the word "cult" is inapt in cases like the ones this article describes, where there'd be no danger in staying or leaving one way or the other. 

On the other hand, I'm a card-carrying cult member of the electronic duo Boards of Canada--which, as it happens, has had a minor preoccupation with cults over the years. I sometimes tell friends who haven't heard of Boards of Canada that it's a musical act whose cult following actually resembles a cult--one that I'm very happy to be a part of and in no hurry to leave.

comments.name: Miss Bear
comments.body:
When, as the poet said, things fall apart, the center cannot hold ... and the center is rotting away, then seed pots do tend to form. Like dandelion seeds to spread out in the wind for new growth which eventually become a new center for new blossoms. Not all of these seeds will grow to fruition, but maybe some will be our future blossoms.

Example: The Pythagoreans were a cult, very problematic for others. Yet some of their notions,  such as the worship of numbers and geometry begat rationality — our dominant mode of being now, altho' usually in a decrepit, dismally mutated status we call capitalism. May new seed pods bring the new and better.

articles.title: ‘Cult’ Used to Mean Something. Now It Applies to Taylor Swift and Trader Joe’s.
articles.summary: The word today applies to more than religious sects, but it says something about our worshipful attitude toward consumption.

comments.name: Mr D
comments.body:
What a selfish and fearful act by the foundation members who approved withholding the use of Mappelthorpe. And what a dishonor to his intention for launching the foundation in the first place. 

Look at his photos. They are beautiful, shocking and brave. The opposite of what his foundation has done.

comments.name: @AJBelanger
comments.body: I agree with those who believe the Mapplethorpe Foundation's actions were understandable and appropriate. I expect even Robert Mapplethorpe would have been shocked to learn how profoundly weak our constitutional protections really are if those in power choose simply to ignore them. Trump's first, and especially his second, presidency revealed that weakness in the starkest terms. With all three branches of government more-or-less in Trump's thrall, there is very little the Mapplethorpe Foundation could reasonably do to defend themselves against ruinous harassment and litigation. Standing on principle against an unprincipled government, in this instance (so an author can use his preferred photo on a book cover), would not be a wise choice of battles to fight.

comments.name: Dani W
comments.body: Funny, I can buy the book, download a copy of the mapplethorpe photo and paste it onto the cover jacket.

comments.name: Robert Skydell
comments.body:
I lived across the street from Roy Cohn's townhouse residence/office in Manhattan during the '70's-'80's and saw him comings and goings. I was aware of his past role as Joe McCarthy's hatchet man but never guessed that he was acting as Trump's mentor until years later.
Mapplethorpe's portrait captures everything one needs to know about Cohn and explains the current mess we find ourselves in.

comments.name: Bob
comments.body: I direct a small not for profit publishing venture attached to a larger nfp institution. If asked your general counsel will assess the risk of the situation the same way every time. In this instance, you don’t ask. Because anyone who works in this sphere will tell you any attempt to strip your status based on this is legally indefensible. This is an easy call. Will you be fighting nuisance suits? Possibly. But here’s the thing. Trump and his cohort don’t read. They don’t look at books. I doubt they know this is even happening. And if they did why would they judge it political/ polemical? I’m sorry but this is a cowardly stance by the Foundation. They have nothing to lose and everything to gain by allowing this. If their resources are so limited they are afraid they’re probably not going to be around much longer anyway. Imagine had they licensed this and the NYT had written a different article. They might have money pouring in for their defense fund.

comments.name: Grandma Emily
comments.body: Yet more evidence that the US is a totalitarian country, fearing reprisals from their government and adjusting their behavior accordingly. Democracy is dead in the US.

comments.name: Richard Barnes
comments.body:
"Its board determined that any kind of government retaliation could drain its financial resources, creating an existential risk for the organization"

This is an appalling decision based out of fear and a desire to not rile the current regime in Washington. The "existential risk" here is not to the financial situation of the Mapplethorpe foundation, but rather to all arts organizations, for profit or not,  under threat of losing their funding because a bully government knows precisely  how to use it's leverage to intimidate causing it to fold. We have been witness to this as universities, law firms, and now arts organizations self censure and surrender. Not to be too dramatic here, but history has shown that this is precisely how autocracies size power. The self censorship is incremental until it's not. This is happening and will continue if we continue to adopt positions such as the Mapplethorpe Foundation board has done here.

comments.name: Mick
comments.body: This really seems quite cowardly and against Mapplethorpe's entire body of work. I do not think he would have made the same decision if he was still around. The contrast between his photo and the one ultimately used is astounding.

articles.title: Roy Cohn, Robert Mapplethorpe and a Trump-Era Dilemma Over Free Speech
articles.summary: When a respected biographer tried to use a Mapplethorpe photograph of Roy Cohn for a book cover, worries about the wrath of Mr. Cohn’s protégé, President Trump, intervened.

comments.name: atibamanii
comments.body: About the worst ticket buying experience I ever had was sleeping on the sidewalk overnight outside the venue to get Rolling Stones tickets for $20?

comments.name: Jeffrey Evans
comments.body:
No mention of Branson MO where some
performers have venues built just for them?

comments.name: Michael James
comments.body: Not mentioned here (at all), but Phish had a great influence on the modern take on residencies...the Baker's Dozen in 2017 (13 nights at MSG, no song repeats).

comments.name: Benign Curmudgeon
comments.body:
In other news the Times didn’t see fit to notice, the greatest entertainer in the world just wrapped his 4th sold out show at MetLife Stadium last night.

Bruno Mars also has a long standing residency in Vegas, which might have been mentioned since not reviewing his spectacular local show.

comments.name: Guido
comments.body: Alas, it reminds me of Tanglewood ...

comments.name: P Aaron
comments.body:
During The Lockdown, Todd Rundgren created a “tour” where he performed many shows in a single location, but broadcast it each night from a supposed different city. The pre-show meal was local food from, say, San Francisco. The audience was a group of TV screens with locals who had bought tickets that were restricted by geolocation (that we circumvented). The stage set had some “local” references including background projections. Each night had its own “Hello, San Francisco!” element to it.

But the stage didn’t have to be broken down each night; the layout could be a bit more complex; the band didn’t have to travel; and, they all got sleep comfortably.

I caught the SF show and the final one. Big TV, great speakers, good tech on his end (because he’s a computer nerd), and a much much cheaper ticket. Except for the crowd ambience, it was a great experience. You can see a bit of these on YT.

comments.name: Jonathan
comments.body: The 'suits' have taken over working class culture.  When I lived in Scotland in the 80's I could go to a football match (stand of the terrace) and a gig that night on a very low wage.  The corporates didn't want to know about working class life!  Now they'd captured it and making life less fun as we can't afford to go to either football or gigs without saving!

comments.name: Jason
comments.body: This is a normal day at the office for Broadway and the West End.  Some shows are only available there and you must travel to see them.  Others may eventually tour, but often with lower production values, let alone different casting.

articles.title: How Residencies Took Over the Music Industry
articles.summary: Harry Styles’s latest Madison Square Garden takeover is part of a trend that some say transfers the cost of touring to fans.

comments.name: Grandma Emily
comments.body: How wonderful! People doing something just for the fun of it, and sharing their joy with others. Bless you!

comments.name: Mar
comments.body:
I’ve been lucky enough to catch a ride or two in a BMW Isetta and seen some of Charles Gould treasures but also (years ago) had the misfortune of driving one of the original Mini Coopers that seemed to stop as soon as it rained.

Not exactly microcars but my current faves would be a Morris Minor or a Nissan Figaro (be still my heart) says this person without a covered garage or mechanical prowess

comments.name: Hitchhiker
comments.body: The Messerschmitt KR200's 'cuter than a June bug' look should give it the right-of-way on the road at all times.

comments.name: Robert
comments.body: When I attended Rider College (1970-1974), my good friend in the dormitory owned a maroon left-driving (Canadian) Mini-Cooper that his mechanic brother had restored and fitted with a Austin-Healy engine transversly mounted.  What a fun ride along the Delaware River scenic byway of Route 29.  Sometimes, we'd tool up Route 206 to Princeton where parking was a breeze.

comments.name: eidrian
comments.body:
I have vivid memories of a German nun, dressed in her habit, coming in a brand-spanking-new BMW Isetta to administer injections to a patient in my building. I always wanted to own a Messerschmitt with the sliding airplane canopy. I had to settle for a K-Car, a Honda Beat, which was the most fun I had on four wheels and always will. It put a smile on my face every time I drove it.
Nowadays, I own and drive a Toyota iQ, aka Scion iQ. Big cars are overrated and totally inconsiderate and selfish, from an ecological point of view.

comments.name: M S
comments.body: Check out the Citroen Ami, a real jewel of a microcar!

comments.name: Nick
comments.body:
I learned to drive in my Mum's Mini in the early 1980's. A manual gearbox made it a lot of fun to drive, at least until I shared the "fun" with my Mum! No more mini for a few weeks!

I loved that car.

comments.name: Thomas Winkler
comments.body: A good friend of mine drove a mini for several years.  He loved it, but I couldn't fit in it!  He and his wife now drive a Honda CRV

articles.title: Pint-Size Cars, With Enviable Smiles Per Gallon
articles.summary: Microcars are underpowered, noisy and sometimes smoky, and it helps if you’re good with a wrench. But “the struggle is what makes it fun,” one enthusiast said.

comments.name: Will
comments.body:
A month ago, the United Kingdom was too dangerous for Harry and his family to visit for even a single day and now they have all moved back indefinitely? 

What changed? Mehgan has an acting gig, so now it's all just fine?

Please. These two are so tiresome.

comments.name: CSE
comments.body: The only observation I will make is that arriving in a private jet, whilst Harry is still waiting for a decision on his security, may not have been the best of choices.  He's a private citizen with money - if he wants to travel that way, his choice. However, the taxpayers of the UK are fighting the government tooth and nail not to have to pay for his estimated yearly armed security cost (if it is granted) of GBP3 - GBP5 million.  The government are dithering - personally, I think they're in a quandary - but some ministers are already making noises that Harry should get it.  Harry had previously indicated that he was willing to pay for it.  I hope he stands by that.  Judging by the articles coming out of the UK, the taxpayers are not happy of any other scenario than Harry or the King paying for it - definitely nothing from the public purse.

comments.name: Christopher
comments.body: It's interesting to share thoughts and feelings - as so many commenters did in this piece. Most comments are from people oblivious to the customs of Britain and the Royal Family. Harry has never read "The Constitution" governing the Royal Family's "performances". I doubt that Meghan Markle even knew of its existence when making sure she married a Royal Prince. Charles has known about the Constitution all of his life knowing from Day 1 what his role was to be as the eldest son of the reigning Monarch. Parliament controls actions of the Royals, stemming from Parliament's beheading of King Charles I (mid-1600s) whose  wife and son were exiled to France for 25 years, while a dictator governed the nation. Parliament then offered the Heir Apparent a return and Accession as King Charles II - and his reign was nothing notable. King Charles III is a weak man and was a weak Heir Apparent. The Royal Family was controlled by the adoption of the Germanic Absolute Primogeniture (that eliminated any female Monarch if there was a male anywhere available.) Queen Elizabeth WAS such a person and rules the longest of any Monarch in UK history, during which time HM changed the Absolutism of Primogeniture to permit Royal women to inherit the throne, but applying only to future Accessions. Harry will create a "Sussex" court, in opposition to the King William V court.

comments.name: Jersey Girl in Texas,
comments.body: Let's put this in proper perspective.  We have Trump making enemies out of our allies, starting wars, destroying our democracy, rigging the next election with everything in his power, took our debt up to $40,53 trillion, orders ICE to attack US citizens in the street and at home, made himself $2 plus billion while in office, and the UK has Harry and Meghan.  No wonder they left.

comments.name: Vicki in Vermont
comments.body: it would be nice for us humans to live and let live.  we do not need to assess the activities of anyone but our own self, and there is little of that and a lot of the other.

comments.name: Alpwalker
comments.body: It will be interesting to see how H&M earn their living now that the one-time Netflix-and-Spare bonanza seems to have faded.  And all the while massive celebrity expenses, including security, continued.  IMO, the creation of new lines of income, and the avoidance of Montecito level expenses are the likely primary drivers for their move.  Which is fair enough - cutting back was probably necessary.

comments.name: Susan Audrey
comments.body:
I hope Harry and Meghan's marriage survives.  She must love Harry very much to agree to move back to UK.  I wonder about her mental and emotional fitness.  HIs too, for that matter.  Perhaps all is being put aside for the children's sake.  Get to know Grandpa, go to schools like Dad, etc.  Meghan is the wild card.  If she can carry on, perhaps they will be successful.

Maybe I shouldn't feel sorry for them, but I do.  Rich and famous yes, but happy and satisfied?  Take (a big one) for the kids.

comments.name: Mary Francis
comments.body:
I wonder if people would be less sympathetic to the royal family’s side of all this were it not for the Catherine and Charles’ dual cancer diagnosis, which came on the heels of the Sussexes departure from “the firm”’and relocation to the US. 

Those medical situations seemed to make it more difficult to criticize the working royals and easier to bash those who’d decided to leave.  

On the flip side, there was little to no sympathy given for the racism Meaghan Markle faced (a known issue in the UK and not surprising for an American interloper who snagged one of their country’s “most eligible bachelors”), nor even a modicum of sympathy regarding the tabloid issues Harry had long railed against (don’t we all kinda get that, hello, remember his mother??).

Just seemed like the cancer stuff (which is awful) tilted the scales towards the royal family and Harry’s side was in a no-win after that.

articles.title: Prince Harry and Meghan Arrive in Britain, BBC Reports
articles.summary: The broadcaster said that the family had landed in the country on Wednesday, without citing sources.

comments.name: Jeffrey
comments.body:
The focus on kids is missing the forest through the trees. The changes should apply to all ages. I don't want the algorithmic feed and was against the initial 2007 attempt to introduce one (Beacon IIRC).

I also resent I need to give any company my age in order to do business. As we know they will abuse that information. Again, we need comprehensive rules for all ages and comprehensive privacy protections.

comments.name: E Plurbis Unum
comments.body:
The competitors should also stop exploiting children.

It is nothing new.  The sexualization of pre-adolescent children (beyond what occurs naturally goes back to the early 60s, and probably 1950s.  Barbie, anyone?

I remember in the early days of finkware, children’s software programs were embedded with more finkware autonomously passing information about your child to anyone who would pay for the information.  Code for 200 embedded discrete finkware codes was common.

I have not the slightest sympathy for Zuckerberg, who ripped his concept off from his roommates, built an empire, helped an operative to download the massive FB information about all US  users and their browsing patterns and triggers - in violation of law and user agreements, that was then used in a massive, hypertargeted disinformation campaign - substantially through target lies on Fb, that probably resulted in a change in administrations in a close race where polls showed a large percentage of the voters for the winning candidate were based on lies, often through FB (or Fox)

For that, Zuckerberg got criticized by one party in committee.

But Zuck is right that other competitors also should not be allowed to victimize children.  Maybe he can convince MAGA that their representatives should support legislation to clamp down, and incidentally, raise Zuck’s reputation a notch.  We know Trump’s only interest in children is that little girls get bigger every day, but he might sign to minimize electoral disaster.

comments.name: D
comments.body:
Attempting legislation or regulation of an industry through a settlement where the settlement amount is conditional upon parties not part of the lawsuit cooperating seems kinda wild. I am not a lawyer but is that actually enforceable? Who is going to enforce it? I bet the legal departments at Alphabet, X, TikTok and every place else encompassed in this “I’ll comply if they comply” are already in the process of getting suits filed to stop what amounts to a tax or levy against them for a lawsuit they were not a part of.

Perhaps the legislators should actually, you know, legislate and (gasp) regulate, because a legal settlement is not the place to be regulating an industry. Other industries have regulations that anyone in that industry needs to follow, it’s the idea of equal protection. If I wanted to enter the garbage hauling business, run a restaurant , or open a gas station I’d need to operate and comply with the correct regulations.

I have an electrician at my house today, he has a license number and is supposed to be competent at doing electrical work according to electrical code. Same way a plumber would need to follow plumbing and gas codes, and be held liable for defective work.

Maybe I’m wrong but this settlement seems to make about as much sense as the idea that Trump and his family can be exempt from taxes.

comments.name: JD
comments.body: We don’t have to view meta as the good guy, but they are right about this.  If other social media companies don’t follow suit, then kids will just go elsewhere.

comments.name: Callie B
comments.body: We need to make the individuals developing these addictive programs responsible for not creating toxic platforms. Meta as a whole is guilty but the individuals who colluded and developed all of the addictive features should have some skin in the game and be made to pay up some of their precious stock if they are found to be developing any app not following the guidelines

comments.name: Jimbo
comments.body: The absolute chutzpah of a billionaire demanding anybody follow the rules is completely laughable.

comments.name: Michael
comments.body: Poor leadership = only doing what is right when others do it too. But Zuck takes it to a more tone deaf and cringy level when he tries to frame this settlement as FB “supporting teens,” waving scraps from his table to state law makers so they go after competitors and make them “play fair.”

comments.name: Scott
comments.body: obviously the rules should apply to tiktok and youtube as well- tiktok is even worse than Meta

articles.title: Mark Zuckerberg Wants to Make Sure His Competitors Share His Pain
articles.summary: Meta, the social media giant, agreed to change the way children interact with its apps. That could be trouble if its competitors don’t abide by the same rules.

comments.name: Gmuon
comments.body: The widespread affection was the result of the actions and causes she took on during her life, as well as of course her musical talents and the great songs that she wrote. Keeping her mouth shut about politics and religion was not the reason people loved her, it was simply how she preferred to deal with it. Let actions speak louder than words.

comments.name: Diane S
comments.body: Dolly was always on the right side of history. All one has to do is look at her life and the things she championed. I feel grateful for getting to see her in Vegas in 1981. I’ll carry the memory of her smiling at me for the rest of my life. RIP Queen.

comments.name: MIMA
comments.body:
We did not care about Dolly’s politics.
We cared about HER! 
We’ll miss her and never stop loving her.

comments.name: RP
comments.body: Americans in general have become too political.

comments.name: Book Maven
comments.body:
Hmm, are these the cautious lyrics of a politically neutral celebrity? Her song writing and her actions spoke volumes about where she stood. 

"Nine to five, yeah, they got you where they want you
There's a better life and you think about it, don't you
It's a rich man's game no matter what they call it
And you spend your life puttin' money in his wallet."

comments.name: Kathy W.
comments.body: That the right and the media did not attack her for her vocal support of immigrants, women’s rights, civil rights, LGBTQ, education, and science WAS NOT BECAUSE SHE WAS NEUTRAL, it’s because attacking a legend who put her Christian values into practice would be a PR disaster for anyone who tried it. Ya’ll trying  repackage all she did and said as “neutrality”  into your made-up sides in a made-up “culture war” is pretty pathetic.

comments.name: Nan
comments.body:
Thank you for this piece on Dolly Parton.  I can see why people could feel a bit let down by how she stayed out of politics. But I remember as a child asking my parents who they voted for in elections and they always replied ... "It is none of your business"     I have to say I doubt that what the current president says is true ..."She really liked me, I will tell you"  because his values are the total antithesis of her values.  But, it is typical of him to make everything about him. 
The world has lost some sparkle now that she is gone.

comments.name: WTR
comments.body: I remember my grandmother would “we don’t talk about religion and politics in mixed company”. Dolly apparently thought this as well. It’s also why everyone loved Betty White. Can we please go back to this time?

articles.title: Dolly Parton’s Cautious Politics Resulted in Widespread Affection
articles.summary: Bipartisan tributes demonstrated the success of the singer’s long-running effort to stay out of party politics in a sharply divided country.

comments.name: Isosceles
comments.body: Can we start calling social media something other than “tech?” I always imagined tech would mean genuine advances in architecture, EV infrastructure, energy, etc. - i.e., feats of engineering worthy of truly moving society forward. Sure the underlying magic of the software involved in social media is an incredible human feat, but this is the end we’ve been putting it toward? What amounts to basically a perpetual online public middle school social experiment? That to me is not “tech.”

comments.name: BC
comments.body:
Settling all these cases for significantly less than Meta's average monthly revenue looks to be nothing more than their cost of doing business. Hopefully they will pay a much bigger price from a big fall in subscribers. 

Given the scale of the problem and the scale of Meta its hard to believe that such a settlement will bother Meta or change its behaviour.

comments.name: Lewis
comments.body: It seems naive to assume that the era of Meta’s dominance is over. A fine like this is just a cost of doing business to them. This is how major corporations operate in America. They pay the fine and then keep doing what they’ve always done. Meta really should be broken up or dismantled completely. It should be nationalized and become a public social media platform with no intention of monetizing its users attention or information.

comments.name: RRI
comments.body:
There is no evidence I have yet read that "the net effects are worse for kids." Don't take that the wrong way.

You are asserting a commonplace assumption. Where are the studies to back up that assumption? There's plenty of evidence it's bad for kids. Thus Meta's capitulation in this case. But why do we let these tech oligarchs off the hook by not focusing on the fundamental harm that, frankly, is their business model, targeting adults with the same addictive algorithmic spew? Why do we not hear, with the same urgency, cited studies of social media effects on adults? Where are they?

Look around you at how adults are behaving, how misbehaving, in our country and try to tell me social media's algorithms for attention grabbing shock value are not having a toxic effect on our lives as much as our children's.

comments.name: TJ
comments.body: I applaud states trying to hold Meta to account, but the problem is systemic. We have created a system of extreme capitalism, where a dollar of profit is worth more than a tree, a bird, oxygen, or even a human life. Until or if we ever address this root cause, these lawsuits are at best, swatting at flies.

comments.name: John from CA
comments.body: Good points,  but why do we give a free pass to most capitalist ventures.  Is the American dream to forever be that those with means get to freely exploit? From our historical roots when indigenous people were purposely sickened with smallpox blankets to our present day AI exploitation, when does the age of irresponsible shareholders and C suiters end? I'm all for capitalism but it's unsustainable if it's primary mantra is caveat emptor.

comments.name: Prof. D.W. Garner
comments.body:
Dear Meta: I am a wizened old guy after 40 years of law teaching  and now I need some real cash. I have been reading media stuff on the computer for years and now my brain seemingly can't remember a thing.  This is surely your fault. 
All reasonable offers are negotiable so how about starting  with a million bucks. As they used to 'baby needs a new pair of shoes'.

comments.name: CinCA
comments.body:
I worked at Facebook many years ago, around the time of the Cambridge Analytica fiasco, and I was honestly blown away by how well-oiled the machine was. Every change to the interface, down to colors, font sizes, spacing, and placement, was rigorously tested and analyzed to understand its potential impact on engagement and revenue.

They were not messing around when it came to figuring out what kept people on the platform, what made them click, and ultimately what made the company more money.

So does anyone really not know that Facebook can be bad for your mental health? The obvious solution is to delete your account. But most people won’t, because the platform is deliberately very good at keeping you there.

    If having power after a blackout or other grid failure is the concern, one needs at least 1,000 watts, and a battery system.
  Used panels are perfectly fine, I have panels for my shop which are recycled from their original installation in 1995.
Used panels are available online at very low prices.
  The other components like charge controller and inverter can, for a small house or strictly emergency use, be bought online for 600-700 dollars together. 
  There really is no point in doing this at all if the scale of it is so small that only a few lights can be operated.
 There is no need to consult a "solar company", they invariably will up-sell everything. Your time on this is best spent on our favorite video-sharing website, where there is an abundance of information on how to do this. There is no substitute for educating yourself. There is nothing complex or difficult about it. And finally, don't fool yourself into believing you can sell power to a utility. It won't work in most places.

Jonathan Haidt’s opinion in “The Anxious Generation” is presciently accurate. 

ERGO 

Meta was very justifiably fined up to $17.1 billion for the following key reasons: 

1. Prioritizing Profit Over Known Danger 
Internal records revealed Meta executives repeatedly ignored warnings from their own safety engineers about platform mechanics designed to act "like cigarettes" for kids. The courts ruled that Meta knowingly traded children’s safety for engagement and advertising revenue. 

2. Illegal Data Harvesting (COPPA Violations) 
Under the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA), it is illegal to collect data on kids under 13 without parental consent. Meta was caught bypassing strict verification—relying heavily on easily faked self-reported birthdates—to actively harvest young kids' data to train its machine learning and AI models.

What a tragedy for those beautiful mountain people. The speed with which water can move and destroy is stunning.

We lived for a while in a small off-grid cabin next to a 20' deep "dry" wash. One evening we heard a loud rumbling that sounded sort of like a large tracked vehicle moving fast down the gravel road that led to town. 

It was only sprinkling at our place but when we went out we could black, black clouds over the mountains where it was obviously pouring. 

We walked down to our bridge that spanned the wash only to see a wall of water at least 6' high, shoving logs and assorted other debris in front roaring down the wash. Within what seemed like seconds, the wash was entirely full of raging, roiling brown water, still carrying huge uprooted trees accompanied by the sound of large boulders rolling along under the flood. In an hour, the water was reduced to a small cafe au lait-colored trickle. 

This is not to imply that our experience was anything close to what those poor folks in the Himalayas are living through. However, is was a graphic example in miniature of what water can do in the mountains.

Craig Childs excellent book, "Secret Knowledge of Water" discusses water in all it's types and forms in the high desert mountains, from ephemeral tinajas to the CO River. He seems to view water as almost a living force to which the deserts must yield and conform. A highly recommended read.

My small community only started funding the Imagination Library a few years ago, after my youngest child had already aged out of the program, so I don't have any direct experience with it.  However, I do have a story.

I was in the public library last month right after story hour.  A little girl, maybe three years old, saw a picture of Dolly and said "I know that lady!"  The library assistant said "You know Dolly Parton?" "Yes!" answered the little girl, "She sends me books!"

What an amazing legacy.

comments.name: Michelle
comments.body:
I grew up in TN and both my kids born in 2006/2009 received books from this program. There is something magical for a child about receiving a book in the mail with their name on it. (Interestingly, they were initially hard back books,)

We found new favorites, such as Bun Bun Button, The Runaway Wok, Read to Tiger, Lissy’s Friends, Officer Buckle & Gloria, and My Lucky Day. I still remember the names because we read them so much! 

When we moved to Ohio I had the opportunity to work with United Way to start the Imagination Library in our county. We started with 5 zip codes and kept raising money till we could cover all the zip codes in our county. 

In 2019, the state partnered with Imagination Library and created the Ohio Governor's Imagination Library to cover half the costs. Since its launch, it has become the state with the highest enrollment with 26 million books being mailed since it was established. Some states have had to make cuts to the program, which means some kids are not receiving books. 

Dolly knew from her father that reading is the foundation for a world of possibilities in your life. I’ve supported the program for years and will continue to do so. 

I believe that it will continue through the generosity of the people who want to help children be the best version of themselves. 

Doesn’t everyone want to be a little more like Dolly🦋???

In a neighboring valley in Nepal after the 2015 earthquake a similar disaster struck: the earthquake dislodged a chunk of glacier (evidently from the same mountain) that fell on and obliterated a village in Langtang National Park. My niece was there traveling during her gap year and was killed. 

The glacial collapse here was much more massive and deadly and wiped out 45 miles of villages and people and terrain, but l've always wondered if the collapse in Langtang that killed my niece was caused by global warming.

Fossil fuel companies have long known about global warming and lied about it. Fox News has given most of its airtime to science deniers turning the whole Republican Party into science deniers too and hobbled our ability to address it. The American Petroleum Institute and Republican governors have sued scholars for suggesting that fossil-fuel companies should help pay for the damage they cause. Such a fund could be used to study Himalayan glaciers, determine which will likely fail, and relocate people who live in harms way. 

Companies like Exxon have known about the science of burning heat-trapping gas and the damage it would cause and lied about it for decades. Exxon has profited on average $60 billion per year even before the Iran War and can well afford cleaning up the mess they made and contributing to a global warming superfund to help these innocent people.

His complaint was totally false, totally fabricated and totally stupid.  They were also hotel guests and he was asked to leave.

comments.name: Welf
comments.body:
That article is missing a few important points. And those explain why the left looses support all over the western world.

Originally the pool was reserved by the Each One Teach One as a private event. They would determine who could enter. Since a association that serves people of African descent this would be black people. Just as any football club or company would do. 

Then the Volksbühne labeled this event as "exclusive for black communities" and asked visitors "to respect this collective self-designation". This was deliberately misleading since it wasn't for black communities, but a specific entity, and there was no need to respect "self-designation", since the entity would decide who comes and not. This imitates the American language of culture wars and provoked backlash from the right. This wasn't coordinated with EOTO, it was done by Volksbühne. Who then got a lot of publicity and support from the urban left. The loser was EOTO, because their event got cancelled. 

The villain in this story is Volksbühne. They sacrificed EOTO for their publicity and their claim of moral superiority. It should be noted that as public institution they - as far as a I know -couldn't even organize an event that enforces racial segregation. But misrepresenting the EOTO event let them have their cake and eat.

comments.name: Mark
comments.body: It is true that some people have greater success in their experiments. There are many reasons why this is so, but at least one of them is about focus. Good experimentalists have intense focus on what they are doing, paying attention to details of their technique (e.g. pipetting) and avoiding distractions such as listening to music or podcasts while they are doing an experiment.

comments.name: danarlington
comments.body: The same thing happens in manufacturing. Work instructions contain terms that are vague, like "shake vigorously" or "don't squeeze too hard." Then there are problems caused by impurities. In one case I know, the "impurity" was essential for success. This was discovered because one supplier failed to follow the instructions, resulting in the impurity. Work by the other supplier, who followed the instructions, failed.

comments.name: edwardc
comments.body:
Rsearchers dealing with animals can have reproducibility problems not discussed in this article or reader comments to date.  

It seems sometimes the sex of the people involved in handling animals, for instance, has been shown to result in different outcomes.

See, for example: 

https://www.understandinganimalresearch.org.uk/news/why-we-need-more-women-in-labs-male-researchers-stress-rodents

https://www.cbc.ca/news/science/lab-mouse-test-results-depend-on-scientist-s-gender-1.2625550

comments.name: MMP
comments.body: Magics hands is also often fraud. An experiment that worked 3 times out of 30 is presented as a breakthrough. Biology is messy but reproducibility is key, and if that is missing, dont attribute it readily to magic. So many papers in so called "glam mags" of biological sciences (Cell, Nature and Science or CNS) are irreproducible because of flimsy fantastical results without rigor being pushed out by editors so as not to miss a "hot" field. Years later (and thousands of hours or even careers or young scientists who try to build upon these results), the field often moves on, but unless there is glaring evidence of data manipulation (like blot cropping), the errors are never acknowledged. This is a real problem in research and AI could perhaps train its sight on algorithmically picking up such problem results which are heralded as break-throughs but often end up too good to be true.

comments.name: TK
comments.body: "Magic hands" almost aways comes down to experience with the protocol, attention to tiniest detail, maintaining details records of everything. 30 years ago I used to run Sanger sequencing reactions using S-35. I went from failed reactions to having "magic hands" in a few months. Soon, the entire lab was asking me for favors. I wish I had saved a few of the autoradiograms, they were beautiful!

comments.name: Joel Fritz
comments.body: Karl Friedrich Gauss developed inferential statistics when he was asked to study measurement errors by astronomical observers.  He developed sound mathematical techniques to predict and analyze frequency of errors and a whole host of other things.  In a quiet way it revolutionized science.  Statistics sidesteps causality.  It's a black box thing that works.  I'm wondering what's going to come out of magic hands studies.  It sounds like something where the methodology will be discussed, uh, thoroughly.  At the same time, if some people are genuinely better at making experiments run well without gaming them it would be highly beneficial to find out how that works.

comments.name: Matt
comments.body: I predict a mix of: (a) some successes, as these guys define success, possibly meeting more of their objective(s), either in minor or major ways; (b) some (possibly) unanticipated effects, such as overlooking results that come from the culture of the lab and parent organization, which may not be replicable; and (c) some surprises, such as new ways to make mistakes.

comments.name: Peter Davis
comments.body:
It's a clever PR hook to talk about 'magic hands' and capturing that lightning in a bottle, but the real story is that scientists are training their robotic replacements, further pushing humanity out of the business of running the world. Given the enormous fears of AI-powered bioterrorism, and the overall uncertainty of real people's place in an AI-driven world, I don't see this as a feel-good story.

And... I spent 15 years in a biology lab and never once heard of 'magic hands'. Yes, some people were good at experimental work, but generally because they worked hard and fast, not because they had amazing technique.
