Looking at the past, we see the present.  Susan Jacobs Dehler’s much praised debut novel STILL explores common elements in the history of women’s lives with a depth that is revealing, not smothering.  The story it tells puts a human face on too often invisible domestic problems and social injustice.  Set with remarkable understanding and artistic detail in the backdrop of larger concerns in our nation’s history (Vietnam, the Great Depression, and the day before 9/11), the life of Mildred Price rolls back and forward in time, telling a different story of the steady undercurrent of small indignities and larger crimes of violence against women. This is a very human, not a sensational novel.  The levers of violence, physical and psychological, are recognizable, and  treated with the significance deserved. Tired of the sameness of celebrity disfunction and romantic escapism, readers will find the hard experiences of the ordinary in our lives will love this book. They will truly see themselves in it.  
The title STILL says much about the past we have experienced. The future is in this book as well, but a question mark must be added to the title to pursue that dimension in our lives.

I applaud anyone who loves classic literature enough to create their own version of it, but I will be avoiding Miss Bates, which apparently has the premise that the REAL Miss Bates is cunning and inwardly "bellowing with rage." That seems a very 21st century take on how a poor 19th century gentlewoman should feel. My goodness, look at all the patriarchy! How can anyone bear it! 

But Jane Austen specifically creates Miss Bates as a character who has been dealt a terrible hand but approaches her lot with an overall feeling of gratitude. ""And yet she was a happy woman, and a woman whom no one named without good-will. It was her own universal good-will and contented temper which worked such wonders." There are people like that out there, but they are rarely captured in books. Most books lean into what people SHOULD feel, not how we find them in the world. 

Catherine Cliff is applying 21st century feminism to Regency England. She can do so of course. But in deciding that her own values must be universal, she kind of reminds me of Mrs Elton in the same book.

comments.name: Mark in Portland
comments.body:
Thank you Jon, for sharing this rich remembrance of one of the greatest bursts of genius songwriting in history ---

-- All the better, as tribute to one of the most luminous human beings, ever, ever -- that has had such a gift.

The greatest music penetrates the listener, without warning if it is the first hearing... 

-- And whenever music at that level includes elements of grief, loss or fear mixed with intense love, it first tears away our defenses leaving us vulnerable and raw, but then immerses us in the comforting realization that someone understands, and cares enough, is strong enough, and is vulnerable enough to lead us there. 

Dolly Parton was that musician, and was that person.

I met her a long time ago... On a spaced-out Sunday afternoon in 1968 avant-garde artist Yayoi Kusama staged a wild, psychedelic happening at Nirvana Head Shop on Union Turnpike, which I managed. It was a surreal slice of counterculture history in the suburbs, featuring nude dancers painted in a polka-dot fashion, and highlighting group-grope psychedelia while doing the boogaloo.

This event perfectly captured Kusama's late-1960s era of "self-obliteration" and "Anatomic Explosions," where she used public nudity and repeating polka dots to challenge conservative societal norms and protest the Vietnam War.
Inside Nirvana, the NYC space-rock band Group Image blasted live music under flashing-colored strobes and black lights. Surrounded by water pipes, posters, and counterculture gear, Yayoi Kusama executed a signature "body painting" happening, covering naked, dancing bodies writhing in glowing polka dots.

The chaotic event was actually the grand finale created by two media pranksters who organized this outrageousness. Joey Skaggs and Paul Krassner created the infamous 1968 "Hippie Bus Tour to Queens" which mocked suburban curiosity about Greenwich Village hippies by taking the hippies to gawk at suburbanites instead.

A massive parade of journalists, including a broadcast crew from The Today Show, followed the bus and documented the entire spectacle.

Here is a reply to my prompt by QWen (LLM controlled by ALiBaba).

The Prompt: Can you suggest a short (by everyone readable) summary of "you control the model, you control its output" and if it is your only source..."?

The Reply: Here is a short, jargon-free summary that anyone can understand:

The Short Summary:
An AI is a locked engine, not a thinking mind. Because its core knowledge is frozen and cannot change on its own, it has no will, agenda, or independent thought.
Therefore, whoever controls the input controls the output.
If the AI is the only source of processing (or information) for a user, then the person who sets the prompts, the system rules, or the training data is the true author of the result. The AI doesn’t
decide what to say; it merely reflects the exact shape of the boundaries you give it.
In short, the model is just the instrument. The controller is the musician.
Why this matters (the "Only Source" implication): If an AI becomes the only source of information or decision-making for a person or organization, then whoever controls that AI effectively controls the narrative, the logic, and the reality presented to the end user. The model doesn't generate truth; it generates what it was controlled to generate.

The ultimate tool to make people alike, or better cloning their cognitive abilities.
